name: Shape Morph
content_range: single obvious transform A:B::C:? (grades 2-3) up to two combined transforms with relational distractors (6-8)
difficulty_levers: transformation type: size, rotation, fill/shade, count, reflection, add/delete element
distractor design: literal-copy, wrong-attribute, over-application foils
one_liner: A first shape turns into a second; the child makes the third shape change the same way by picking the matching fourth.
interaction: The top row shows A with an animated morph arrow into B. The bottom row shows C, an arrow, and an empty slot with 4 options below. The child taps the option that is to C what B is to A; it snaps into the slot. An optional two-icon confidence tap (a star for sure, a wavy hand for not sure) appears, then GO submits.
self_teach: The ghost-hand replays the A-to-B morph (e.g., big shrinks to small), then applies the same shrink to C and taps the matching option; the analogy row lights up. Warm-up: big circle to small circle, so big square to ? (small square).
engagement_hook: A magic morph - watching A visibly transform into B and then casting the same spell on C is playful and makes the hidden rule tangible.
tail_precision_rationale: M-ERRTYPE uses a designed distractor set - a literal-copy foil (no transform applied), a wrong-attribute foil, and an over/under-application foil - so a wrong answer reveals exactly where the relational mapping broke and grades how far below the analogy cut a child sits. On two-rule items the same distractor keying feeds the proposed M-RULEID (how many transformations were correctly applied), separating one-rule from two-rule mappers at the tail. M-RTFIRST captures the map-before-act latency typical of strong reasoners, and M-CONF on a subset removes lucky guesses via confidence-accuracy calibration.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Exclude K-1 to avoid measuring the relational shift instead of reasoning; include a literal-copy foil so surface matching does not score; pair shade/color with shape; keep the confidence tap optional and non-punitive; big tap options remove motor load; the ghost-hand morph plus warm-up controls novelty. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Clue Detective
content_range: two positive single-feature clues over four candidates (grades 2-3) up to conjunctive and relational spatial clues over six-plus candidates (6-8)
difficulty_levers: clue polarity (positive vs negated) and logical form (single vs conjunctive)
relational/spatial clues (inside, above) vs simple attribute clues
how much each clue prunes (forcing more inference per step)
one_liner: A lineup of figures hides one culprit; clue cards flip over one at a time and the child crosses out every figure a clue rules out until only the answer is left.
interaction: Six candidate figures sit in a lineup. Clue cards (wordless icons, e.g., a crossed-out blue swatch = not blue; a hole icon = must have a hole) reveal one at a time. After each clue the child taps the figures it eliminates (they dim and get an X); a mis-eliminated figure can be tapped again to restore it. When the child believes one figure survives all clues, they tap it in a final SELECT slot to answer. Eliminations are process-scored; the final pick is the keyed answer.
self_teach: The ghost-hand reveals the first clue card, then taps the two figures that clash with it - each dims with an X - and shakes its head at a figure that fits (leaving it lit). The warm-up runs a two-clue puzzle with obvious color/shape clues so the eliminate-the-violators loop is felt once before scoring.
engagement_hook: A whodunit: each flipped clue card lets you rule out suspects, and the detective satisfaction of narrowing six figures down to the one culprit keeps kids leaning in.

M-ERRTYPE tags whether errors come from mishandling negation (not-blue) vs conjunction, and M-REV flags confident, targeted revisions vs thrashing.

name: Investigation Station
content_range: one-variable investigations with an obvious outcome (young) up to multi-variable systems requiring controlled comparison and trade-offs (older)
difficulty_levers: number of manipulable variables, noise in the outcome, whether the best answer requires controlling confounds, depth of the required conclusion

The engine logs which combinations are tested (breadth), whether successive tests change one thing at a time to be informative, the full test sequence, progress toward the answer over trials, and a rubric score for the reasoning in the final conclusion. self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a hand setting a low ramp and releasing the ball (short roll), then raising only the ramp and releasing again (longer roll), then tapping the 'it went farther' result - cueing 'try things, watch what happens, then say what you found.' name: Mystery Gate
content_range: single obvious-feature gate with a tiny feature palette (grades 2-3) up to conjunctive/relational hidden rules over many varying dimensions (6-8)
difficulty_levers: size of the hypothesis space (number of features that vary)
rule form: single feature to conjunction to relational
number of allowed tests before I KNOW IT
one_liner: A magic gate opens only for figures that follow a secret rule; the child builds their own figures to test, watches which pass, then uses what they learned to judge new figures.
interaction: The child assembles a test figure from a small feature palette (tap to set shape, color, and count), then taps SEND to push it through the gate; the gate glows and opens (accept) or buzzes and bounces it back (reject), and the figure drops into an ACCEPTED or REJECTED tray. The child runs as many self-chosen tests as they like. When ready they tap I KNOW IT, and three probe figures appear one at a time; for each the child taps the OPEN gate (belongs) or the CLOSED gate (does not) to classify it. A hint lamp reveals one extra accepted example. Only the three final classifications are scored; the tests are the process record.
self_teach: The ghost-hand builds one figure on the palette (two taps), sends it, and the gate opens with a green glow and the figure lands in the ACCEPTED tray; it then builds a second figure that the gate buzzes and bounces into the REJECTED tray, making accept/reject obvious wordlessly. The warm-up uses a blatant one-color rule so the child feels the test-then-learn loop once before scoring.
engagement_hook: You are a scientist running experiments on a magic gate - every figure you invent is a little test, and the thrill of cracking the secret rule with a clever probe is intrinsically rewarding.
tail_precision_rationale: Because the child designs their own experiments, M-HYP (informativeness of each self-chosen test) and M-EFF (tests used vs the minimum needed to disambiguate) isolate strategic inductive reasoners far more sharply than final accuracy: two children can both classify the probes correctly yet differ by running 3 controlled tests vs 12 confounded ones. M-PROG turns the test stream into an uncertainty-reduction curve (a dynamic-assessment learning-rate signal), M-PATH records the exact experiment sequence for evidence-model scoring, and hint-free discovery (M-HINT) is stronger evidence at the ceiling.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Audit that the accept-set uniquely identifies the rule so M-HYP is meaningful; cap or de-emphasize test count so trial-and-error flooding is not rewarded (M-EFF penalizes it); pair color with shape/count so color-blind children are not disadvantaged; keep hints non-punitive but logged; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; exclude K-1 to avoid a floor that would misread as low ability. name: More or Fewer
content_range: large-ratio comparisons with small arrays and generous exposure through close-ratio, larger-array, brief-exposure comparisons under incongruent continuous visual cues
difficulty_levers: distance from the child's fitted threshold
one_liner: The child taps the side that flashed more dots.
interaction: Two dot clouds appear simultaneously for a brief calibrated exposure, disappear behind neutral covers, and leave two large side buttons. Array ratio adapts while dot size, density, total area, convex hull, and color relationships are counterbalanced.

M-DIFFREACH records the closest ratio solved under cue-balanced conditions, and M-CONSIST guards against side-biased or noisy estimates. M-RT and M-SPEEDACC are interpreted only with accuracy so impulsive fast taps receive no advantage, while M-ACC across many balanced trials anchors the psychometric fit.

Exposure must be frame-timed across devices and long enough for visual access but short enough to discourage counting. Screen glare, visual impairment, and color vision require high-contrast achromatic defaults; raw speed is never scored without accuracy. name: Make It Equal
content_range: small dot-group non-canonical equalities through multi-operation compensation, decomposition, repeated-group, and unknown-position equivalence structures
difficulty_levers: one versus multiple operations across both sides
concrete quantity support and degree of fading
compensation, decomposition, inverse, or repeated-group structure
one_liner: The child places the missing quantity that makes both sides of the equal sign match.
interaction: Two sides appear around a large equal sign, each backed by a faint two-pan balance; quantities are dot groups or numeral-plus-bar tiles and joining or removing is shown with simple action icons. engagement_hook: Every solved equality steadies a glowing bridge between two islands, making same-on-both-sides physically satisfying.

M-ERRTYPE preserves compensation, inverse-operation, side-confusion, and near-miss evidence, while M-REV records spontaneous correction before commit without requiring an explanation. name: Machine Rule

difficulty_levers: constant versus input-dependent or alternating rule
one_liner: The child watches what a machine does to quantities and chooses what it will make next.
interaction: Two to four example trays show an input quantity entering a machine and an output quantity emerging; a final input enters and the output tray remains empty. name: Number Web
content_range: single-relation 2x2 quantity analogies with concrete magnitude tiles through 3x3 webs requiring several co-acting additive, multiplicative, partition, inverse, or composed relations
difficulty_levers: one to three simultaneous row and column relations
relation family and number of transformation steps
missing-cell position and amount of redundant evidence
distractors violating one versus several constraints
one_liner: The child finds the quantity tile that completes every connection in a number web.
interaction: A 2x2 analogy or 3x3 web has one glowing empty cell and 4-6 candidate quantity tiles. Quantities are shown as segmented bars, grouped dots, or numerals paired with a magnitude strip; relation arrows animate only during the demo and carry no labels. The child taps one tile to place it, may swap it, and taps the central web button to submit, with no typing or reading.
self_teach: A wordless ghost hand traces a two-dot tile becoming a four-dot tile across the top row, traces the same connection from three dots to the empty cell, and taps the six-dot answer; the completed web glows, all in under 10 seconds. One unscored single-relation 2x2 warm-up follows with corrective animation before scored items.
engagement_hook: The web behaves like a circuit: the correct quantity closes every glowing connection and sends a pulse around the grid.
tail_precision_rationale: M-RULEID and rule-keyed M-ERRTYPE turn a hard web into relation-level evidence: a child satisfying two of three constraints is distinguishable from one applying an unrelated rule. M-DIFFREACH identifies the maximum matrix size, relation family, and simultaneous rule count solved, while M-RTFIRST captures time spent encoding the full web before acting. M-LEARNRATE across novel relation families helps separate rapid abstraction from practiced arithmetic, and M-ACC anchors the adaptive estimate.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Matrix familiarity, numeral fluency, and visual clutter can contaminate performance; use the ghost-hand warm-up, pair symbols with magnitudes, and keep connectors sparse. Arithmetic facts must stay easy relative to the target relation count. name: Explorer's Map

one_liner: The child explores a foggy top-down world that reveals only what is nearby, then shows they built a map in their head by pointing back toward hidden landmarks and taking a shortcut they never walked.
interaction: A top-down world is covered in fog that clears only around the child's avatar as they tap adjacent tiles to walk, uncovering paths and landmarks (a tree, a well, home). difficulty_levers: number of cars; syntactic complexity (SVO to embedded and relative clauses); distractor orderings in the recognition variant; picture-plus-audio versus printed word; frequency band of the words

name: Bubble Pop Memory (n-back / dual n-back)
content_range: 2-3 single 1-back at a gentle pace up to 6-8 dual visual-plus-auditory n-back at higher n
difficulty_levers: n level; single versus dual channel; bubble pace; target and lure rate
one_liner: Bubbles float up one at a time showing a picture, and the child taps POP whenever the current bubble matches the one from n bubbles ago; a dual mode adds a sound channel.
interaction: Bubbles rise at a fixed pace, each showing a shape or colour; the child taps a POP button when the current bubble equals the one n steps back (single stream). Dual mode plays a chime or shows a letter alongside each bubble with a separate SOUND-POP button, and the child responds to either channel independently. Taps do not advance the stream. n rises when signal-detection sensitivity is high (about 80 percent) and falls when it is low, pushing each child above grade level; scoring is sensitivity- and consistency-based, never raw speed.
self_teach: A wordless 1-back ghost-hand demo shows two identical bubbles in a row and the hand tapping POP with a check (about 6s), then an unscored 1-back warm-up; the rising-bubble rhythm and the POP button read instantly with no text.
engagement_hook: A bubble-popping arcade where you pop only the bubbles that repeat from n-ago; faster streams and a second sound channel make leveling up feel like a real challenge.
tail_precision_rationale: A continuous updating stream is rich in tail telemetry: signal-detection sensitivity (M-DPRIME) separates true match detection from response bias, lure false alarms (M-FALSEALARM at n plus or minus 1) expose fragile temporal binding, the accuracy-by-load slope (M-UPDATECOST) indexes updating efficiency, and the highest sustained n (M-DIFFREACH) probes capacity above grade level; RT variability (M-RTVAR) scores worst-performance consistency rather than impulsive speed.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Attention and ADHD are the dominant confound: continuous updating loads sustained attention and impulse control, so bias-free d-prime is reported, consistency is weighted over speed, and scores are gated on engaged blocks. A fixed pace can clip slow responses (generous response window). Novelty is mitigated by the warm-up. The auditory channel uses a visible letter so muted or deaf and hard-of-hearing children are not disadvantaged. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

metrics.name: Item accuracy
metrics.what: Correct / incorrect (dichotomous) on a scored item.
metrics.how_to_collect: Log final response vs key per scored item.
metrics.usefulness_tail: The base IRT signal; at the tail, accuracy on very hard items is the primary separator once difficulty is high enough to avoid ceiling.

metrics.name: Signal-detection sensitivity (d-prime)
metrics.what: Signal-detection sensitivity (d-prime)
metrics.how_to_collect: From hits and false alarms compute d-prime = z(hit rate) minus z(false-alarm rate) with standard edge corrections.
metrics.usefulness_tail: Separates true match-detection sensitivity from response bias in continuous tasks, so a cautious child and a guesser are not scored alike near the cut.

metrics.name: Commission / false-alarm rate
metrics.what: Commission / false-alarm rate
metrics.how_to_collect: Count taps on non-target/foil stimuli plus anticipatory responses faster than a plausible floor (<150 ms), divided by response opportunities.
metrics.usefulness_tail: Isolates impulsive fast-but-wrong responding so raw speed is never rewarded; separates careful-fast (able) from impulsive-fast responders and underlies the concentration-performance index.

metrics.name: Updating cost
metrics.what: Updating cost
metrics.how_to_collect: Regress accuracy (or RT) on memory load / update count and take the slope.
metrics.usefulness_tail: The accuracy or RT decrement per additional to-be-updated item or level indexes the efficiency of gating and replacing WM contents, a purer executive signal than static span.

metrics.name: Intra-individual RT variability
metrics.what: SD or coefficient of variation of RT across items.
metrics.how_to_collect: Compute SD/CV over the child's RT series (correct trials).
metrics.usefulness_tail: Consistency (low variability) tracks ability better than peak speed (worst-performance rule); a strong, less-coachable tail signal.

metrics.name: Ceiling / max difficulty reached
metrics.what: Highest item difficulty answered correctly.
metrics.how_to_collect: Track max b-parameter solved under adaptive escalation.
metrics.usefulness_tail: Directly probes the tail; adaptive escalation to failure pinpoints the child's edge and is the sharpest single tail statistic.

name: Claim Duel
content_range: one-strong-one-irrelevant concrete claims (4-5) up to abstract claims with subtle weak-but-related lures and multi-step warrants (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: evidence-relevance subtlety (strong vs weak vs thematic lure)
requirement to supply a warrant linking data to claim
one_liner: The child props up a claim by dragging the strongest evidence cards to it and knocks down a rival claim by picking its weakest link.
interaction: A claim card is shown with a pool of evidence cards (some strongly relevant, some weakly/irrelevantly related, some off-topic). The child taps evidence cards to attach them to the claim, building the strongest support; then in a duel a rival claim appears and the child taps the evidence that best rebuts it. Strength meters fill by link quality. Picture/icon-supported cards with short audio labels keep reading load low. No typing.
self_teach: The ghost-hand taps the on-topic strong-evidence card onto the claim (its strength bar fills green) and skips the off-topic card (which greys out) - under 10s, showing attach strong evidence, not weak. One unscored warm-up with one clearly strong and one clearly irrelevant card runs before scored, subtler items begin.

name: Build-It Buddy
content_range: One- or two-step placements of large pieces (K-1) up to multi-step directions with embedded spatial, relational, and color conditions (6-8)
difficulty_levers: number of steps; embedded conditions per step; relational and spatial complexity; piece count on the tray; single replay allowed
one_liner: Listen to step-by-step spoken directions and build the picture by dragging, placing, and coloring the pieces so it matches what was described.
interaction: An empty canvas plus a tray of pieces (shapes, animals, colors) is shown while audio gives a multi-step construction direction (put the red square in the top corner, then put a star under it, then color the tree green). The child performs each step by dragging a piece to a location, placing it, or tapping a color; a replay repeats the audio once. Unlike selection tasks the child constructs the arrangement from scratch. Steps lock on submit and are auto-scored against the described end-state as partial credit; the number of steps and embedded conditions adapt up after success (an above-grade span staircase).

name: Proof Hunt
content_range: Two-panel picture stories with one-step inference (K-1) up to multi-paragraph literary/informational passages needing global or author's-purpose inference and multi-sentence evidence (6-8).
difficulty_levers: passage length; inference depth (literal -> bridging -> global -> author's purpose); number of evidence sentences required; strength of the plausible-but-unsupported evidence lure; listening vs reading.
one_liner: Answer a question about a short story, then tap the exact part that proves your answer.
interaction: A short passage is shown (audio + 3-4 comic panels for pre-readers; printed text split into tappable sentences for older bands). Step A: an inference/main-idea question appears with picture or text choices and the child taps an answer. Step B: the child taps the sentence(s) - or the comic panel - that is the evidence for that answer; selected text highlights and can be toggled off. Submit locks both parts. Scored as a two-part evidence-based selected response: full credit needs the right answer AND the right evidence.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): a two-panel scene plays (a child holds an empty lunchbox and frowns); the question shows two faces, the hand taps the hungry face, then glides to the empty-lunchbox panel and taps it so it glows as the 'proof'. One unscored warm-up runs before scoring.
engagement_hook: A detective mechanic: answering is 'making the accusation' and highlighting the evidence 'proves the case' - the passage flashes a magnifying-glass stamp and a 'Case Solved' badge only when answer and proof agree.

M-INFDEPTH records the deepest inference layer a child can support with correct evidence, and M-PATH (which sentences were tapped, in what order) plus M-ERRTYPE (chose a plausible-but-unsupported sentence vs an off-topic one) reveal near-misses that mark latent ability just under the cut.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Reading decoding can confound comprehension at older bands (mitigated by a listen mode and by the picture-panel evidence version for young bands); highlighting UI could add motor/selection noise (large sentence hit-boxes, toggle-to-deselect, revisions logged via M-REV/M-PATH); background knowledge (balanced, novel-world topics); the evidence step is language-light (tap, not type) to protect ELL children. name: Sentence Sense
content_range: 3 picture-plus-audio cards forming a simple SVO sentence (2-3) up to 6-8 word printed cards forming multi-clause sentences with a grammatical-but-absurd lure (6-8)
difficulty_levers: number of cards; syntactic complexity (SVO to embedded clauses); closeness of the absurd ordering to the sensible one; picture-plus-audio versus printed word; word frequency leveled so rare vocabulary does not confound syntax
one_liner: Drag the scrambled word cards into order to build the sentence that makes sense - not the silly one that breaks the rules of the world.
interaction: Word cards (picture-plus-word for young bands with audio labels; frequency-leveled printed words for older) appear scrambled on a rack. The child drags them into a track to form a sentence. The same words can form more than one grammatical order, but only one is sensible (the cat chased the mouse) while the other is absurd (the pizza ate the boy is impossible, or the mouse chased the cat is world-implausible in the framed scene); the child must build the sensible one. An optional second tap on the leftover silly reading marks why it is silly. Cards snap into slots, can be re-dragged (a revision), and lock on submit; scoring credits adjacent-pair order plus semantic plausibility.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): three scrambled cards (chased / cat / mouse with a the) are dragged into the cat chased the mouse and the scene plays it out; the reversed silly order wobbles and is rejected. One unscored warm-up (dog / the / barks) runs before scoring.
engagement_hook: A word-builder where snapping the cards into the sensible order makes the scene come alive and act it out, while the silly order makes a goofy impossible cartoon - so getting it right is the funny payoff.
tail_precision_rationale: Ordering yields graded credit (M-POLY by adjacent-pair correctness), turning one item into many bits, while the plausibility contrast adds inference depth (M-INFDEPTH: did the child reject a grammatical-but-absurd reading) that pure arrangement misses. The drag log (M-PATH) and re-drags (M-REV) separate decisive planners from shufflers, and M-ERRTYPE distinguishes a grammatical-but-silly ordering (semantic near-miss, latent ability) from an ungrammatical scramble, sharpening placement at the cut.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Sentence building is language- and exposure-loaded (mitigated by picture-plus-audio cards for young bands, frequency leveling so syntax not rare vocabulary carries difficulty, and ELL-neutral frames); world-knowledge plausibility can be cultural (universal physical and biological scenarios); drag motor demand (large snap slots, free re-dragging, M-REV logged so fumbles are not scored as errors); reading load only in the older printed mode (audio labels available). name: Story Order
content_range: 3 wordless picture panels in obvious time order (K-1) up to 5-6 sentence strips ordered by causal necessity with a global 'why' inference (6-8).
difficulty_levers: number of parts; time-order vs causal-order; similarity/interchangeability of parts; picture vs sentence strips; presence of prediction and 'why' probes.
one_liner: Put the mixed-up parts of a story in the right order, then choose what happens next.
interaction: Three to six story parts appear scrambled - picture panels for pre-readers, sentence strips for older bands. The child drags them into a track to make the events make sense (temporal/causal order). name: Question Quest
content_range: simple single-oddity scenes (young) up to rich scenes with many possible questions and subtler anomalies (older)

one_liner: Shown a strange, intriguing picture, the child asks as many questions about it as they can and guesses what caused it and what might happen next.
interaction: An odd scene appears (a door in a tree, a puddle that glows). The child builds questions by tapping starter cards (Who / What / Where / Why / How / What if) and finishing them, or types them freely; separate rounds invite 'guess why this happened' and 'guess what happens next.' The engine logs the number of questions, their depth (surface what/who vs causal why/how vs hypothetical what-if), and the fluency and variety of the cause and consequence guesses. Every question and guess is welcomed; none is wrong.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows the scene, then a hand tapping the 'Why...?' card and a question bubble popping up, then a 'What if...?' card with another bubble - cueing 'ask lots of questions about it.' One unscored warm-up scene lets the child ask two questions before scoring.
engagement_hook: A mysterious scene that begs 'what is going on here?', where every question the child asks lights up the picture and reveals a tiny hint - curiosity is immediately rewarded with a peek behind the mystery.

name: Sorting Robot
content_range: Concrete taxonomic categories such as animals vs non-animals (K-1) up to abstract/superordinate and functional or cross-domain word categories (6-8).
difficulty_levers: category abstractness (perceptual -> taxonomic -> functional/superordinate); closeness of boundary exemplars and competing-category lures; number of demonstrated examples before testing; picture vs printed word; word frequency (Zipf band).
one_liner: Watch a robot drop a few example pictures or words into its IN bin or OUT bin, figure out the hidden category rule, then sort new items IN or OUT yourself.
interaction: A friendly robot has a green IN bin and a red OUT bin. It first demonstrates by dropping two or three labeled examples - positive examples fall IN, negative examples fall OUT - revealing a hidden semantic category (for example, animals go IN and non-animals go OUT). Then new item cards are handed to the child one at a time; the child taps IN or OUT (or drags the card into a bin). An optional 'peek' lets the child test one example to see where the robot files it (a scored hint). Correct sorts snap with a chime and the robot's happy meter fills; the round ends after a fixed set. Audio names each item for pre-readers; older bands use frequency-leveled printed words and more abstract, superordinate, or functional categories. This is category-rule induction from examples, not picking a fourth member or ejecting an odd one.
self_teach: Wordless ghost-hand demo (<10s): the robot drops a dog IN, an apple OUT, and a cat IN (the hidden rule is 'animals'); a new fish card appears and the hand taps the IN bin so it snaps in.
